title: Baby-proofing and child-proofing a home, by room and by age

notes.text: The 'ages' labels are scoping words. A label is source-backed only where a source states an age (for example gates until at least 2 years [10], laundry packets and children 6 and under [23, 25], crib to toddler bed at about 35 inches [20], no helmet or bike travel under 1 year [16], back seat to 13 [7], recommendations for babies up to 1 year [0]). Other labels are generic stage words (babies, crawling and walking children, young children) and not numeric claims. Clinician to confirm before any age-gating in the app.

items.text: Unsafe sleep
items.detail: Back to sleep, firm flat level surface (never inclined), bare sleep space, never on an adult bed, sofa or armchair, room share without bed sharing.

items.text: Drowning
items.ages: leading cause of death at 1-4y; second leading cause of unintentional injury death at 5-14y
items.detail: Arm's reach, four-sided 4 ft fence with self-latching gate, never alone in the bath, life jackets.

items.text: Firearms
items.detail: Safest is no gun; otherwise locked, unloaded, ammunition locked separately.

items.text: Poisoning (medicines, cleaners, laundry packets, nicotine, cannabis, alcohol)
items.detail: Lock up, original containers, call Poison Help 1-800-222-1222, do not induce vomiting.

items.text: Button batteries and magnets
items.ages: young children, and teens for magnets
items.detail: Out of reach; if you suspect a child swallowed a battery, or one is in the nose, ear or throat, go to emergency care or call 911 straight away; if a magnet may have been swallowed or has hurt a child, call your pediatrician or go to the nearest emergency department straight away.

items.text: Falls (stairs, windows, furniture, carriers)
items.detail: Gates, window stops (no more than 4 in; the UK NHS says under 6.5 cm / 2.5 in, so aim for the smaller gap), carriers on floor, harnesses.

items.text: Furniture and TV tip-over
items.detail: Anchor to wall or floor.

items.text: Choking
items.detail: Cut food to half-inch or smaller, round firm foods only fully chopped, supervise meals, keep small parts and balloons away.

items.text: Strangulation (blind cords, drawstrings, cords)
items.detail: Cordless blinds, secure cords, no pacifier cords, no drawstrings on playgrounds.

items.text: Burns and scalds
items.detail: Water heater at or below 120F (49C), hot drinks out of reach, screens on heaters.

items.text: Vehicle heatstroke
items.detail: Never leave a child in a car; look before you lock.

items.text: Fire and carbon monoxide
items.detail: Working smoke alarms on every level and in bedrooms; CO alarms near sleeping areas.

items.text: Write down and leave: parents' numbers, neighbour's number, pediatrician, fire/rescue, police, Poison Help (1-800-222-1222), home phone and home address.
Leave each child's date of birth and approximate weight, plus any allergies or special needs (for medical staff).
Say where you will be and when you expect to be back; the sitter should call or text if any question arises.
Walk the sitter through the house: fire exits, hazards, flashlight, first aid supplies; if there is a fire, leave at once and call the fire department from a neighbour's house or a mobile phone.
Explain feeding, bathing and bedtime arrangements; for babies, show the safe sleep set-up (on back, bare crib).
Sitter does not give medicine or food unless parents instruct; never leaves children alone, even briefly; does not open the door to strangers.
Make sure any guns are unloaded and locked with ammunition separate (ideally none in the home).
If the sitter drives, provide the correct car or booster seats.
Sitter minimum: the AAP page says at least 13 and mature enough for common emergencies; confirm first aid and CPR training and meet them beforehand.
Grandparents and other carers: check that they have made their home safe too (locked medicines, purses out of reach, no walkers).
Remind visitors and sitters to keep purses and bags (with medicines) out of reach.
Put baby on their back for every sleep, naps and nights, including babies with reflux. Side sleeping is as dangerous as stomach sleeping.
items.detail: Lowers SIDS and sleep-related death risk.

items.text: Use a firm, flat, level sleep surface that is not tilted at all: a crib, a bassinet, a play yard or a portable crib made to safety standards, with only a snug fitted sheet.
items.detail: Soft, tilted or raised surfaces can block a baby's breathing (positional asphyxia). The CDC, NICHD and Health Canada all call for a flat, level surface with no slope, so no slope at all is the safe choice.

items.text: Do not use inclined sleepers, hammocks, crib wedges, nursing pillows, loungers or baby nests for sleep, and do not use any product for sleep that is not made for infant sleep. Any alternative infant sleep product must meet the federal (CPSC) infant sleep standards.
items.detail: Products that tilt or cradle a baby can let the head slump or the body slide into a position where breathing is blocked.

items.text: Keep pillows, blankets, quilts, bumper pads, positioners, soft toys and weighted items out of the sleep space. Dress baby in one more layer than an adult would wear, or use a wearable blanket. Do not put a hat on baby indoors or cover their head.
items.detail: Suffocation, entrapment and overheating.

items.text: Keep the baby's sleep space in your room, near but not in your bed, for at least the first 6 months.
items.detail: Room sharing is linked to as much as 50% lower SIDS risk (AAP, NICHD).

items.text: Do not bed share. The AAP says to avoid it under any circumstances; room sharing without bed sharing is safest. Never fall asleep with baby on a sofa or armchair.
items.detail: AAP: the risk of sleep-related death is 5 to 10 times higher when sharing a bed under 4 months, more than 10 times higher after alcohol, drugs or sedating medicine, and up to 67 times higher on a couch, soft armchair or cushion.

items.text: Never let baby sleep on an adult bed, couch, sofa, armchair, waterbed, air mattress or futon, whether alone or with someone else. If baby has dropped off on one of these, move them to their own flat sleep space.
items.detail: Soft adult surfaces make SIDS and other sleep-related deaths more likely, and a baby can be trapped or smothered; couches and armchairs are especially dangerous if an adult dozes off on them.

items.text: If baby nods off in a car seat, stroller, swing, carrier or sling, lay them on their back on a firm, flat surface as soon as you can.
items.detail: Slumped upright sleep can block breathing.

items.text: If you use a sling or carrier, keep baby's face visible at all times, keep them close and upright with the chin off the chest, and do not feed baby in it (take them out first). Do not zip a coat around baby in a carrier.
items.detail: Suffocation and overheating.

items.text: Swaddling is optional and does not lower SIDS risk. If you swaddle: always on the back, not too tight, and stop as soon as baby looks like they are trying to roll (often 3-4 months, sometimes earlier). Never use weighted swaddles.
items.ages: until baby shows signs of rolling
items.detail: The risk of suffocation is higher if a swaddled baby rolls onto their stomach (AAP).

items.text: Offer a pacifier for naps and at bedtime (if breastfeeding, wait until it is well established). Do not hang a pacifier on a cord or clip it to clothing.
items.detail: Pacifiers lower SIDS risk (AAP, CDC). A cord or clip can strangle a baby. The AAP bars neck cords and clothing clips during sleep and the NHS allows a clip only while an adult is watching, so using neither is the safest rule.

items.text: Check cribs and used cribs for recalls, missing hardware and instructions; do not use a broken crib. Lower the mattress as baby grows; consider a toddler bed at about 35 inches tall or when the child starts climbing out.
items.ages: until climbing out or about 35 in
items.detail: Falls out of cribs and crib failure.

items.text: Keep the room smoke-free; no smoking or vaping around baby. Room about 16-20C (UK guidance); check for overheating (sweating, hot chest or flushed skin).
items.detail: Smoke exposure and overheating raise SIDS risk.

items.text: Do not use baby walkers. Use a stationary activity center, play yard or high chair instead.
items.ages: infants (no age range is given by the sources)
items.detail: Walkers can roll down stairs, let a child reach hot or poisonous things, and the AAP says they can delay when a child starts to walk.

items.text: Anchor TVs, TV stands, bookcases, dressers, shelves, desks and chests to the wall or floor.
items.detail: Young children climb on furniture and TVs, lean on them and pull themselves up, and the furniture can tip over and crush a child.

items.text: Pad or remove sharp-cornered furniture (coffee tables are a particular hazard) from walking areas; put corner and edge bumpers on furniture and hearths.
items.detail: Head and face injuries from falls against sharp edges.

items.text: Screen fireplaces, wood stoves, space heaters, hot radiators and hot vents. Fireguards should enclose the whole fire or heater and be fixed to the wall; barriers should have the lowest point of their top edge at least 56 cm (22 in) off the floor.
items.detail: Contact burns.

items.text: Cover unused outlets with plugs too big to be a choking hazard; use tamper-resistant receptacles when replacing; keep cords out of reach.
items.detail: Electrical injury and cord pulling.

items.text: Check floors at a child's eye level for coins, beads, buttons, pins, pills and small toy parts; keep older children's small toys separate from babies and toddlers.
items.detail: Choking and ingestion.

items.text: Know which devices use button or lithium coin batteries (remotes, key fobs, thermometers, flameless candles, musical cards, hearing aids) and keep them out of reach; tape battery compartments shut. Batteries can also lodge in the nose or ear. Post the National Battery Ingestion Hotline number (800-498-8666) with your other emergency numbers.
items.detail: A lithium coin battery stuck in the oesophagus can burn through it within 2 hours. If you suspect a child has swallowed one, or a battery is in the nose, ear or throat, go to an emergency department or call 911 straight away; serious damage can happen quickly.

items.text: Keep loose magnets, especially small high-powered ones, and magnetic toys with small pieces away from children. The AAP urges families with children not to keep high-powered magnet sets at home and to get rid of any rare-earth magnets; otherwise keep small or loose magnets in a locked container up high. Check magnetic toys often for cracks.
items.ages: babies, toddlers and older children (including teens)
items.detail: If more than one high-powered magnet is swallowed they can pull together inside the body and cause serious damage. Symptoms can include stomach pain, vomiting and fever, which are common in children, so a swallowed magnet may not be obvious. If a magnet may have been swallowed, or a child has been hurt by one, get in touch with your pediatrician or go to the nearest emergency department straight away; waiting can lead to severe injury.

items.text: Know the plants in your home and yard; consider removing poisonous ones or keeping them out of reach. Poison Help can tell you which plants are harmful.
items.detail: Poisoning.

items.text: Fit a gate at both the top and the bottom of the stairs once baby starts to crawl and walk. At the top, use a gate that screws to the wall or studs, not a pressure-mounted or accordion-style gate; check the gate is rated for top-of-stairs use. Do not use pet gates.
items.detail: Falls; accordion and V-shaped gates can trap a head or neck.

items.text: Keep stair gates in place until the child is at least 2 (UK guidance); close the gate every time.
items.detail: Falls continue as children learn to climb.

items.text: Hold the handrail when carrying a baby; keep stairs clear of toys and clutter and well lit. If stairs are carpeted, tack the carpet down firmly at the edges. Consider anti-slip rugs, and do not let a child run around in socks on hardwood floors.
items.detail: Adult falls while carrying a baby, and slips.

items.text: Use door-knob covers or locks on rooms you do not want children to enter (covers must still let an adult in quickly in an emergency). Fasten glass doors open; remove swinging and folding doors until the child is old enough to grasp how they operate.
items.detail: Access to hazardous rooms and finger and hand injuries.

items.text: Cover banister or balcony gaps wider than 6.5 cm (2.5 in) with boards or safety netting (UK NHS guidance).
items.detail: Head and body entrapment and falls.

items.text: Fit window guards or stops so windows open only a small gap (screens do not stop falls). Aim for the smallest gap: US and Canadian pages say no more than 4 inches (10 cm), and the UK NHS says under 6.5 cm (2.5 in), so the NHS figure is the safer target. Guards must still be openable by an adult or older child in an emergency, so keep at least one usable escape window in each room, and make sure adults know where any window keys are kept.
items.ages: from when a child can crawl and climb
items.detail: Falls from windows. The 4 in (10 cm) and 6.5 cm (2.5 in) limits come from different countries; the smaller gap is the safer choice.

items.text: Open double-hung windows from the top, keep them locked and closed when not in use, and move cribs, chairs, sofas, low tables and other climbable furniture away from windows.
items.detail: Children climb furniture to reach windows.

items.text: Prefer cordless blinds and shades. If you keep corded ones: anchor cords with floor mounts or wall brackets, add stop devices, cut looped cords and add safety tassels, shorten pull cords, and keep cribs and beds away from cords.
items.detail: Strangulation.

items.text: Lock cabinets and drawers holding cleaners, medicines, matches, lighters and knives; keep products locked even if the packaging is child-resistant.
items.detail: Poisoning, cuts. Child-resistant packaging slows children down but is not child-proof.

items.text: Use the back burners and turn pot handles inward or to the back. Keep hot drinks well out of reach (a drink can still scald a child a quarter of an hour after it was made), put a hot drink down well out of reach before holding a baby, and use cups with tight-fitting lids.
items.detail: Scalds.

items.text: Install anti-tip brackets on freestanding ranges and stoves. Choose a cordless kettle, or one whose flex is short or coiled.
items.detail: Tip-over and cord pulling.

items.text: Warm milk in a bottle warmer or a jug or pot of hot water, not the microwave (hot spots); test a few drops on your wrist before feeding.
items.detail: Scalds from uneven heating.

items.text: Use a harness (the NHS describes a 5-point harness) in high chairs, strollers and prams every time; set carriers and bouncers on the floor, never on counters or tables.
items.detail: Falls.

items.text: Child-resistant lids or out-of-reach bins for trash with spoiled food, razor blades and batteries. Knot plastic bags (including dry-cleaning bags) before discarding.
items.detail: Ingestion and suffocation.

items.text: Cut up food for babies and young children so that no piece is bigger than half an inch, and teach them to chew well. Keep high-risk foods (hot dogs, whole grapes, raw carrot sticks, nuts and seeds, chewing gum, hard or sticky sweets) from children until about age 4 or older depending on development; round firm foods may be served only if completely chopped into tiny pieces. Children sit to eat; supervise meals.
items.ages: from starting solids; high-risk foods to about 4y
items.detail: NHS: food is the most common thing babies and toddlers choke on. AAP: small round objects (balloons, balls, marbles, toy pieces and round foods) cause the most choking deaths.

items.text: Never leave a baby or young child alone in the bath, even for a moment, even if an older brother or sister is in the bath with them. Bath seats and rings are not safety devices. Empty the tub right after use.
items.detail: Drowning can happen in seconds and silently, in very shallow water.

items.text: Set the water heater to 120F (49C) or lower, or fit anti-scald devices on faucets and shower heads. At bath time run cold water in first, then add hot; check the temperature with your elbow or wrist before the child gets in; bathe the child away from the faucets; take them out of the tub before running more hot water.
items.detail: Scalds.

items.text: Use non-slip mats or decals in the tub and shower.
items.detail: Slips.

items.text: Lock up or keep out of reach all medicines, including any in purses and bags.
items.detail: Poisoning. The NHS lists medicines first among causes of hospital admission for poisoning in under-5s.

items.text: While children 6 and under live in or visit the home, use traditional liquid or powder detergent rather than single-use packets. If you keep packets, keep them in the original container, locked and high up, not on or under the washer or dryer.
items.detail: Packets are concentrated, look like candy and can cause serious breathing, stomach and eye injuries.

items.text: Never mix detergent with ammonia or other cleaning products (some mixtures release dangerous fumes); keep the laundry room door shut and locked whenever you are not in there.
items.detail: Toxic fumes and curious children getting in.

items.text: Keep chemicals and cleaning products in their original containers; never transfer them into another container, especially a food or drink container.
items.detail: Mistaken ingestion.

items.text: UK: keep liquid laundry capsules, dishwasher tablets and toilet gel discs out of sight and reach, and pick cleaning products with a bittering agent added (it makes them taste unpleasant).
items.detail: Poisoning and chemical burns.

items.text: Keep medicines locked (a locked toolbox works). If anyone in the home takes opioids, lock them away and have naloxone on hand; dispose of unused medicines.
items.detail: Overdose and self-harm risk. AAP: every child can be at risk.

items.text: Lock up alcohol and empty unfinished drinks straight away.
items.detail: Alcohol is very toxic to a young child; alcohol use can increase impulsive harm in young people.

items.text: Keep liquid nicotine (vaping e-liquid) and cannabis edibles locked or out of reach, in original child-resistant packaging, apart from normal food.
items.detail: Even a small amount of liquid nicotine can be fatal; edibles can look like sweets.

items.text: If a child or teen may be thinking about suicide, put knives, razors, belts, ropes and similar items somewhere secure, and be ready to take the locks off bathroom and bedroom doors (the AAP says this may be necessary). Call or text 988 (US). Talking about suicide does not make it more likely to happen. If a child talks about hurting themselves, get help right away: phone their doctor or go to an emergency department.
items.detail: Reduces access to lethal means during a crisis. The AAP says pediatricians now look for depression and suicide risk in every child at checkups from age 12.

items.text: The safest home for a child has no gun; remove firearms from the home if you can. If there is one: store it unloaded in a locked case or safe, ammunition locked separately, and keep keys and combinations away from children and teens.
items.detail: Even toddlers are strong enough to pull a trigger; teen risk includes impulsive self-harm.

items.text: Do not rely on hiding the gun or on teaching children not to touch it.
items.detail: Children are curious and kids have found guns their parents thought were well hidden; many studies show teaching alone is not enough.

items.text: Do not leave a loaded or unlocked gun in a car or anywhere on the property.
items.detail: Access outside the home.

items.text: Stay within arm's reach of a young child in or near water, with no phone or alcohol distractions, even if a lifeguard is present or the child has had swimming lessons.
items.detail: Drowning is the top cause of death for ages 1-4 and the second most common cause of accidental injury death for ages 5-14 (CDC).

items.text: Home pools: a four-sided fence, at least 4 feet tall, enclosing the pool completely and keeping it apart from the house, with a self-closing, self-latching gate. Add layers such as self-closing, self-locking doors or door alarms, pool alarms and a power safety cover, and re-establish the barrier after every use. When nobody is using the pool, take out any toys that could draw a child in.
items.detail: Barriers cut unsupervised access.

items.text: If a child is missing, check the pool first.
items.detail: Seconds matter.

items.text: Fence, fill in or securely cover garden ponds; empty and store paddling pools straight after use. Drowning can also happen in bathtubs and water-filled buckets, so stay with a child near any standing water.
items.detail: Children can drown in a few centimetres of water.

items.text: Use a properly fitted US Coast Guard-approved life jacket on boats and around open water. Floaties, arm bands and water wings are not safety devices.
items.detail: Inflatables slip off and create false security.

items.text: Never leave a child alone in a car, even briefly; a cracked window, shade or air conditioning does not make it safe. Look in the back seat every time, put your phone or bag in the back, and ask your caregiver to call if the child is more than 10 minutes late.
items.ages: all children (heatstroke is the biggest non-crash vehicle killer of children under 15)
items.detail: A car can warm about 20F in 10 minutes; a child overheats 3 to 5 times as fast as an adult; heatstroke can occur when it is as cool as 57F outside.

items.text: Keep cars locked when parked, keys out of children's reach, and rear fold-down seats closed. Teach children that cars and trunks are not play areas.
items.detail: Children who climb into cars can lock themselves in (AAP: 1 in 4 hot car deaths).

items.text: If you notice a child alone in a car and are worried, call 911 straight away. If the child is unresponsive or in pain: call 911, get them out of the car and spray them with cool water (never an ice bath). If the child is responding to you, remain with them until help comes.
items.detail: Emergency response.

items.text: Use rear-facing as long as the seat allows, then a forward-facing harness seat as long as possible (at least to age 4), then a belt-positioning booster until the seat belt fits (about 4 ft 9 in tall, typically 8 to 12 years), then the seat belt; children under 13 ride in the back seat.
items.detail: Crash protection by size.

items.text: Never run a car or truck in a garage attached to the house, even with the garage door open. Run generators only outdoors, over 20 feet from any window, door or vent; never inside the home or garage, even with doors and windows open.
items.detail: Carbon monoxide.

items.text: Smoke alarms on every level including the basement, inside each bedroom and outside sleeping areas; interconnected if possible; test monthly; replace the whole unit every 10 years; change non-sealed batteries at least yearly.
items.detail: Early warning.

items.text: Carbon monoxide alarms outside bedrooms near every sleeping area, battery-operated or with battery backup; replace per the manufacturer or every 5 years; check batteries when clocks change.
items.detail: CO is a poison gas you cannot see or smell.

items.text: Practise a fire escape plan; tell sitters to get out at once if there is a fire, then call the fire department from a mobile phone or a neighbor's home.
items.detail: Children cannot plan an escape alone.

items.text: Playground surface: a thick layer (12 or more inches) of wood chips, mulch, sand or pea gravel, or safety-tested rubber mats, reaching 6 feet or more out on every side; not concrete, asphalt or grass. Platforms higher than 30 inches that are meant for school-aged children need guardrails or barriers. Supervise actively.
items.detail: More than 200,000 children a year are treated in emergency departments for playground injuries (CPSC figure quoted by AAP); most injuries are falls, so the surface under the equipment matters.

items.text: Avoid drawstring sweatshirts and necklaces on the playground, and keep jump ropes and pet leashes off the equipment; take off helmets before playing on equipment; choose shade, as metal and plastic slides get hot enough to burn.
items.detail: Strangulation and burns.

items.text: Bicycle helmet that meets the CPSC standard, sitting level on the head with the top of the forehead covered. The child should be able to see the helmet brim when looking up, and the chin strap should be snug. Replace after a serious crash and about every 5 years. Neither helmets nor bike travel are recommended for babies under 1.
items.detail: Head injury.

items.text: The AAP advises against home trampolines altogether; if one is used, limit jumpers to one at a time.
items.detail: Thousands of injuries a year, especially under age 6.

items.text: Before a child plays at another home, ask about supervision, pools (4-foot four-sided fence with self-latching gate), trampolines, firearms (unloaded, locked, ammunition separate), screens and pets. For sleepovers, ask who will be in the home; a 'lateover' (home at bedtime) is an option.
items.detail: Risks outside your control.

items.text: Back to sleep on a firm, flat, level surface in your room (not your bed, and never an adult bed, sofa or armchair); nothing soft in the sleep space; smoke-free home.
Do not bed share; the AAP reports sleep-related death is 5 to 10 times more likely when a baby under 4 months shares a bed.
Never leave baby alone on a bed, sofa or changing table; keep carriers and bouncers on the floor.
Install the car seat rear-facing before the first ride home; never leave baby in a car.
Check bath temperature with your elbow or wrist and stay with baby throughout; never leave baby alone in water.
Set the water heater at 120F (49C) or lower; keep hot drinks away from baby.
Smoke and CO alarms working before baby comes home.
If you use a sling or carrier, keep baby's face visible and do not feed in it.
Stop swaddling at the first signs of trying to roll; move to a wearable blanket.
Keep room sharing to at least 6 months; keep the crib clear even as baby rolls.
Gates at stairs once crawling; anchor furniture; cover outlets; secure blind and other cords.
Check floors at eye level for small objects such as coins, buttons and small toy parts.
Keep coin and button batteries and loose magnets out of reach.
Lock cleaners and medicines; keep purses up; no walkers.
Harness in high chair and stroller; carriers on the floor.
Cut foods into pieces no larger than half an inch; avoid high-risk choking foods.
Window guards or stops, and furniture away from windows, once climbing starts.
Anchor TVs and furniture to the wall or floor.
Constant arm's-reach supervision near any water, including baths and water-filled buckets; fence pools.
Lock up everything toxic: laundry packets, e-liquid, cannabis, medicines, alcohol, button batteries, loose magnets.
Move to a toddler bed at about 35 in or when climbing out.
Keep the car seat rear-facing as long as the seat allows.
Stove: back burners, handles in; hot drinks out of reach.
Window guards or stops that limit the opening to a small gap (no more than 4 in / 10 cm; the UK NHS says under 6.5 cm / 2.5 in, which is the safer target); cordless blinds.
Food cut to small pieces; seated eating; serve round firm foods only if completely chopped.
Forward-facing harness seat as long as possible (at least to age 4), then a booster; back seat.
Keep high-risk foods modified until about age 4 or later, depending on chewing skill; balloons are a choking risk to about age 8.
Swim lessons plus continued close, constant supervision; floaties are not protection.
Helmet for bike riding; teach that cars and trunks are not play places.
Keep laundry packets away until all children in or visiting the home are at least 6.
Check playground surfacing and remove drawstrings.
Ask about guns, pools and supervision before playdates.
Belt-positioning booster until the seat belt fits (about 4 ft 9 in, often 8-12 years); seat belt fit check; back seat until 13.
Helmet for bike riding, replaced after a crash and about every 5 years.

Water: drowning is the second most common cause of accidental injury death at ages 5-14, and about 40% of drowning deaths at these ages are in natural water; life jackets on boats and around open water; swim lessons help but do not replace supervision.
Online safety: most-secure privacy settings on new accounts, rules on who to chat with, open talk that they can come to you, a family media plan, screen-free times.
Ask other parents about firearms, supervision, pools and screens before sleepovers; consider a 'lateover'.
Do not rely on talking to the child about guns; lock them up. Do not let children take a turn shooting a firearm.
Start talking with your child about alcohol around age 9 and keep the conversation going through elementary, middle and high school.
Every child can be at risk of suicide: keep medicines, alcohol and firearms locked in every home.

ageBands.note: Insufficient verified material for this band beyond the items above. No opened source covers kitchen and stove independence, being home alone, bullying, or age limits for online accounts. Clinician or educator to supply before this band is treated as complete.

items.text: Teen driving: seat belts every trip, graduated licensing (supervised practice, limits on teen passengers and night driving), no impaired or distracted driving; parents can set rules stricter than state law.
Lock up firearms (unloaded, ammunition separate, keys and combinations away from teens); teens face higher unintentional and self-harm risk.
Lock up medicines and alcohol; keep naloxone in the home (AAP: especially households with teens, and always if anyone uses opioids).
Online safety: ongoing conversation, privacy settings, understanding who you talk to; family media plan.

Talk about drugs and alcohol early and often, outside the heat of the moment, starting with open-ended questions and connection rather than control; counterfeit pills sold as Xanax, Percocet or Adderall can contain fentanyl. Tell your teen they can always call or text you for a ride, no questions asked.
Talk to teens about the risks of fake magnetic piercings in the mouth or nose; they can be swallowed or inhaled.

Tell your pediatrician about shifts in mood, sleep, appetite, school work or friendships; from age 12, pediatricians look for signs of depression and suicide risk in every child. Crisis support: 988 (call or text, US).

ageBands.note: Insufficient verified material for this band beyond the items above. No opened source covers vaping or cannabis specifics beyond locking up and talking early, sexting or sextortion, mental-health care pathways beyond screening and 988, or when teens may be home alone. Clinician or educator to supply before this band is treated as complete.

helplines.name: Emergency (unconscious, not breathing, seizure, swallowed button battery)
Poison Help (free, confidential, any poisoning question)
988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline (call or text 988; chat also available; free, 24/7)
Crisis Text Line (text HOME to 741741; keyword as shown on the service's own site)
NHS 111 urgent medical advice (includes help for a child under 5)
NHS 111, mental health option (urgent mental health help: choose the mental health option when you call 111)
Samaritans (free, any time; listening service, UK and Ireland)
Emergency (child unconscious or struggling to breathe)
9-8-8 Suicide Crisis Helpline (call or text, any time of day, every day)
Poisons Information Centre (open all day and night, from anywhere in Australia; call 000 in an emergency)
Lifeline crisis support (confidential, 24 hours a day; call 000 if life is in danger)
